cues.why: The ordinary night outside the settlement, from the chapter's first line until the moment Jack looks out of the window. It exists to be UNREMARKABLE: a normal night behind the glass while the alarms and the vibrations happen indoors, so that what replaces it lands.

Civil sirens across the settlement, heard indoors. Procedural rather than recorded because the recorded one did not loop cleanly -- it was even for 5.5 of its 12 seconds and announced its own seam every time it wrapped. This one closes its phase exactly at 12 s. EMPHASIS -4.4 dB: Joshua asked for the sirens 40% quieter, and only the sirens, so it is a per-cue nudge rather than a move of the whole alarm category, which would have taken the console alarm bed he tuned by ear down with it. LEVEL -10 dB and the high end filtered away: Joshua heard it as beside them rather than outside. Distance is both, not either. LEVEL -18 dB total: still too loud at -10, so another 60% off. LEVEL: -4.4 read as too loud, -10 still too loud, -18 vanished entirely. -14 bisects the last two. A siren is a TONE, and a tone carries far further than broadband noise at the same RMS, which is why the category target alone kept missing it.
The manuscript opens on his hands. Loudest of the typing cues because it is the first sound of the chapter.
Sarah at the secondary console, working the interrupt.
NEW. The shake arrives before the narration names it, so the listener feels it with Sarah rather than being told about it.

"...the emergency sirens outside changed pitch." They did not: the same siren kept playing under the line that said it had changed, which Joshua caught. The first pattern stops on the previous line and this one comes in 1.2 s into the sentence, under the words themselves. Higher and faster, so it reads as the town escalating rather than as a different recording. LEVEL -10 dB and the high end filtered away: Joshua heard it as beside them rather than outside. Distance is both, not either. LEVEL -18 dB total: still too loud at -10, so another 60% off. LEVEL: -4.4 read as too loud, -10 still too loud, -18 vanished entirely. -14 bisects the last two. A siren is a TONE, and a tone carries far further than broadband noise at the same RMS, which is why the category target alone kept missing it.
NEW asset, second use, quieter. The manuscript calls it another vibration, so it should be the same sound diminished rather than a new one.
Into the gap before Scale factor locked. Reused.
NEW. The event. It ends in real silence rather than a tail, because the manuscript is explicit that the sound does not fade or become muffled, it ceases to exist.
NEW. The other half. The silence between the two is carried by the manifest's own pauses across the four narration segments in between, so the quiet is real rather than printed into a file.

Reused. The alarms run from the landing to the sentence that stops them, and their stopping is what leaves the silence the scene needs. EMPHASIS DROPPED TO 0 on 2026-09-19. The +6.0/+8.3 here were raising the one sound Joshua said he could not hear the narrator past, and they were chosen when the mix was placed by RMS -- which reads this asset 3 to 6 dB quieter than the ear does. With loudness measured properly the category target is already where this moment should sit.
Reused. The room tone returns alone into the silence the alarms left, and stays for the rest of the chapter. After the event it is the only thing that sounds normal.
Jack checking whether TOMBS is off. Quiet work in a quiet room.
NEW asset, reused from chapter 2. Lena getting through is the first contact with anyone outside the room since the event.
Reused. The channel stays open through the communications check and closes on the sentence where Jack lowers his wrist.

THE SOUND OF THE WORLD CHANGING, on 'He looked outside.' The night bed stops and this takes its place and holds to the last line of the chapter. The settlement has not moved and nothing outside has actually started making a new noise -- but the hills are grass now, and the listener is told that by the air rather than by a line of dialogue. Nine and a half minutes long, so it never reaches a loop seam inside the scene it covers.

On 'He looked outside.' -- the same instant the forest bed comes in. The sirens have been distant all chapter; here the attention goes through the glass and they are briefly THERE, louder on purpose for a few seconds, and then they wind down and fade out completely. What is left is the world, which is the point of the scene: the last human sound gives way and the listener is alone with something enormous. Joshua asked for exactly this shape -- louder for a few seconds, then winding out to let silence and the background take over. EMPHASIS +6 dB: at 0 it sat 23 dB under the narration, which is not 'louder on purpose'. It is meant to be the one moment the sirens are close.
Reused. The cameras answering is the mechanism by which the chapter shows the scale of what happened.
Reused, quieter. One more feed, and the drop of water.

NEW, and the most important new asset in either chapter. The first sound of the giant world, arriving from outside with no seismic cause. It plays before the narration so the listener hears it exactly as Jack and Sarah do: an event first, an explanation never.
NEW asset, second use. The manuscript brings it back and then lets it go, and Jack decides he is not certain he wants to know what it was. The same sound twice is the whole point.
Reused. One final record remains, and the machine reports the scale factor as calmly as it reported everything else.

_comment: Ambience was switched OFF on 2026-09-18 while Joshua had no bed he liked, and back
ON the same day when he supplied one: amb_computer_lab, a real recorded computer
room. Both the browser and the exported mp3 read this switch, so the page and the
file always agree.
To supply more: story-rules/reference/SUPPLYING_AMBIENCE.md. Every supplied file
must carry a credit block -- validation refuses one without it.
Where each kind of sound sits in the finished mix, in dBFS RMS, with the narration
running about -22. scripts/audio.py retune-cues derives every cue gain from these
and the asset's MEASURED level, so a gain survives its asset being regenerated or
renormalised instead of silently becoming wrong.
Set after Joshua listened to the first normalised build and said the sound was
super loud. He was right and the numbers said so: nine cues sat at or above the
narrator's own level, including amb_tombs_array_power_rise -- a bed running under
whole chapters at -21 to -23 dBFS -- and two deep vibrations at -18.8, louder than
the voice. That is what happens when assets are lifted 20 to 27 dB and the gains
that were rescuing them are left in place.
A cue may carry `emphasisDb` in its cue sheet to sit above its category, and the
cue sheet is where such a decision belongs: it is about that moment in the story.
LOWERED 3.1 dB (30% in amplitude) on 2026-09-18: Joshua, on the retuned build, still
found the sound too loud against the voices. Applied to every category so the layer
moves as one and the relationships between cues stay as they were.
LOWERED A FURTHER 6 dB on 2026-09-18, third pass. Joshua, after the 30% cut: SFX
still too loud. Beds now sit about 29 dB under the narration and one-shot events
about 23. If that turns out to be too far, raise these five numbers -- nothing else
needs to change, because every gain is derived from them.
AMBIENCE LOWERED A FURTHER 55% (-6.9 dB) on 2026-09-18 before being switched off,
so that whenever it comes back it starts where Joshua asked rather than where the
last pass left it.
A TONE IS NOT A NOISE, and this table targets RMS as though it were. A 500 Hz sine
at -50 dBFS is plainly audible where a broadband bed at -50 is not, so the sirens
needed roughly 14 dB more attenuation than the table gives -- not because the table
is wrong for beds, but because RMS is a poor predictor for anything tonal. When a
future asset is a tone, expect its emphasisDb to be large and negative.
SUPERSEDED on 2026-09-19 by categoryTargetLufs. Kept as the fallback for an
asset measured before loudness was recorded; the retune report names any cue
still landing on it as 'rms fallback'. When no asset reads that way, delete it.
The DRAMA exports. They were 192 kbps STEREO built from sources that are almost
entirely mono -- paying twice the bitrate for a second channel carrying the same
signal. 96 kbps mono is the same audio at half the size: 36.3 MB becomes about 18.
THE VOICE-ONLY EXPORTS ARE DELIBERATELY NOT TOUCHED. combine joins the clips with
`-c copy`, which is lossless and fast, and re-encoding 500 seconds of narration to
save nine megabytes would spend quality on the one thing the whole project is for.
The silence between clips must also stay at the clips' own format or the copy-join
breaks, which is a good reason not to make that number configurable at all.
Raise these if a stereo mix ever becomes real; nothing else needs to change.
Where each kind of sound sits in the finished mix, in LUFS -- BS.1770
integrated loudness -- with the narration at about -20. scripts/audio.py
retune-cues derives every cue gain from these and the asset's MEASURED
loudness, so a gain survives its asset being regenerated or renormalised.
THIS TABLE REPLACES categoryTargetDbfs, AND ONLY THE MEASURE CHANGED. The
numbers are carried across unaltered on purpose: an asset whose RMS and
loudness agree does not move at all, and the ones that do move are exactly
the ones the old measure was placing wrongly.
Joshua, 2026-09-19: 'The first alarm sound in the first chapter is louder
than the narrator's voice... can't hear him talking.' The cue sheet had it
17 dB under the narration and the file disagreed: sfx_console_alarm_erupt
reads -11.5 dBFS RMS and -5.6 LUFS, so it arrived 5.9 dB louder than the
mix believed. Across the whole set RMS minus LUFS runs from +5.6 to -13.1,
an 18.7 dB spread -- while for speech the two agree within a decibel, which
is why measuring effects against a speech reference by RMS looked right for
as long as it did.
The old note here told a future asset that is a tone to expect a large
negative emphasisDb. That advice stands for the SIRENS, whose RMS and
loudness agree to within 0.1 dB and which are intrusive for reasons
loudness does not measure -- but it was the wrong explanation for the
alerts and notify tones, and those no longer need an emphasis at all.

timeline.source: each segment's pause then its clip; the same sum the exports are built with

mixed.indexSource: the manifest timeline, which the mix is built from

voice.indexSource: none: an mp3 -c copy join cannot be addressed by the arithmetic, and summing the parts overstates it because the demuxer applies each clip's gapless padding. Measured, chapter one runs 3.2 s longer than the sum says while a part-by-part index drifts 12 s -- so this file is offered for download and listening, never as something the page indexes into.
